uniequip_002_ray:
Human Resources Record File RF-099-47
Day One
Operator Ray has been reported missing this morning without submitting any official application to leave the ship. Human Resources is currently collaborating with Field Operations to investigate.
Day Two
While the Field Operations team conducts searches, we have also reviewed Ray's recent activities. On the night before her disappearance, she attended a private dance, which we consider to be abnormal behavior. We interviewed Alanna, Ray's friend and an intern at the Workshop, for more details. Below is an excerpt from our interview:
'To think a weirdo like her went to a dance! I would never have believed it was her, but her cookie-shaped bangs were too iconic.'
'What did she do at the dance?'
'Umm... She just sat in a corner. Now that's more like something she'd do.'
'Did she get into contact with anyone during the dance?'
'Well, there was this old lady with a cane who sat in the corner with her.'
'Did they interact in any way?'
'That's the strange part! Neither of them spoke at all. It was as if they weren't at a dance, but sitting in a sauna house!'
Day Three
According to our investigation, the elderly woman whom Ray interacted with is a retired Operator from the Logistics Department currently on Rhodes Island for Oripathy treatment. She provided the following explanation for her attendance at the dance:
She used to be a dance teacher in her youth but had to end her career prematurely due to Oripathy. Now, severe crystallization of her left leg requires her to use a cane for walking.
Statement from Retired Operator: 'All I wanted was to see young people dance.'
Day Four
After another futile day of searching, the search party witnessed two 'blue ghosts' as they were about to return. The Field Operators quickly assumed battle formations but broke formation after carefully probing said 'ghosts' with Arts: One of them was Ray.
Next to Ray was a wasteland burdenbeast, its thick skin folds glistening with a blue hue as it heaved and twisted its massive body, as if dancing. Ray, also covered in a blue light, remained motionless. However, she was smiling like a child—a rare sight.
[Supplementary Information]
Ray later learned that the blue light came from the dust pheromone of the Fluorescent Originium Slug, which causes intolerable irritation upon contact with the skin. This explained why the burdenbeast appeared to be dancing; in reality, it was writhing in itchiness. As for why Ray could remain unaffected by the itch... her 'excellent' rating in physical resilience is well-deserved. Below is an excerpt from our interview with her:
'So, why did you suddenly leave the ship?'
'I wanted to find the big burdenbeasts on the Columbian wasteland and make them dance to the moon again.'
'Err... Did this have anything to do with the dance you attended? Was it because of the old lady who sat next to you?'
'Yes. Her eyes showed me that she wanted to dance. So I suddenly felt that it was time to let the burdenbeasts dance again.'
'... Huh?'
'Yup.'
'Well, umm, did you ever meet that old lady again? Maybe you'd like to tell her about your experience?'
'No... but you're right, that'd be nice. If it's not too much trouble, could you tell her for me?'
uniequip_003_ray:
The very first time Rayella saw a sandbeast was during a long, arduous winter. Not a single drop of water had sputtered out of the geyser over the last five months, and the entire barrens were devoid of animal life. The hunters, who refused to provoke the giant metal crabs no matter what, grudgingly set their sights on the dunes where the sandbeasts dwell.
Even the most experienced of hunters had difficulty telling which dunes were natural, and which were sandbeast burrows. Even if they did manage to find a burrow entrance, actually catching the beasties was mostly up to luck. As the hunters busied themselves burying their heads in the sand, far away, under a dried-up bottletree, Rayella saw a sandbeast's backfin softly swaying. It calmly used its tongue to scoop up the young musbeast trying to escape between its fangs, contentedly rubbing its hooves against the tree roots, like it didn't care one whit about anything going on around it. The bitter winters of Rim Billiton's barrens might have been a terrible thing for the hunters, but to the sandbeast, it was just an ordinary winter day.
The young Rayella was unaware of just how important the life-saving meat of this sandbeast was. She couldn't stop herself from revering that little creature she had never seen before. She did not tell anyone else about what she saw that day.
The second time Rayella saw a sandbeast was in a dark, dingy shed. Metal cages of every size covered every inch of the shed that wasn't a walkway, and the sound of claws scraping against steel was more ear-piercing than the fiercest barrenlands wind. The animals that once inspired reverence in her were here in the hundreds, crowded into the cages. She could not help but wonder if they were going to be used to hunt musbeasts, or help plow the soil. As it turned out, neither. The network of capillaries running through their backfins made them perfect for testing for poisonous gases in mines, like a natural test strip.
This time, Rayella spoke up. She'd seen these animals before, and she said that she knew what they could actually do. She saw it herself, after all.
'Still, they've got those backfins, right?' The shop owner replied nonchalantly, as if what the sandbeasts could do and where they could go didn't matter. Rayella suddenly froze. How her dad had scolded her in the name of the family they had to bury that winter, she couldn't quite remember.
And so, many years later, when pitsinker Ray got a piece of coated paper saying 'Certificate of Qualification' from a mine foreman with good intentions, she had no idea he was trying to help her out. It was tough work, but Ray was just barely able to read the lettering on it, which said she was certified to do... something. She had zero idea what use it would be. As luck would have it, when she got home, she saw the sandbeast had nipped yet another hole into the roof of its kennel. She made a crease in the middle of the paper, carefully gluing it to the top of the kennel.
Whatever opportunity that piece of paper might have opened up for her, she will never know. What she does know is that with a solid roof over its head, the little fella won't catch a cold at night. As for its food for next week and hairball meds for the next month, she'll come up with something.
At the very least, the morning wind, laden with dawn mist, will be able to point the way for her.
